claim: Streptolysin O (SLO) is a bacterial toxin which forms temporary pores in the membrane.
source: Site-specific fluorescent labeling of proteins inside live mammalian cells has been achieved by employing Streptolysin O, a bacterial toxin which forms temporary pores in the membrane and allows delivery of virtually any fluorescent probes, ranging from labeled IgG's to small ligands, with high efficiency (>85% of cells).
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a characteristic of SLO.

claim: SLO allows delivery of virtually any fluorescent probes with high efficiency (>85% of cells).
source: Site-specific fluorescent labeling of proteins inside live mammalian cells has been achieved by employing Streptolysin O, a bacterial toxin which forms temporary pores in the membrane and allows delivery of virtually any fluorescent probes, ranging from labeled IgG's to small ligands, with high efficiency (>85% of cells).
evidence: The abstract provides a specific quantitative measure of delivery efficiency.

claim: The whole process, including recovery, takes 30 min.
source: The whole process, including recovery, takes 30 min, and the cell is ready to be imaged immediately.
evidence: The abstract states the total time required for the procedure.

claim: When combined with Oxyrase, a ~20x improvement in fluorescence photostability is achieved.
source: When combined with Oxyrase, a cell-friendly photostabilizer, a ~20x improvement in fluorescence photostability is achieved.
evidence: The abstract provides a quantitative measure of photostability improvement.

claim: By adding glutathione, fluorophores are made to blink, enabling super-resolution fluorescence with 20–30 nm resolution over a long time (~30 min) under continuous illumination.
source: By adding in glutathione, fluorophores are made to blink, enabling super-resolution fluorescence with 20–30 nm resolution over a long time (~30 min) under continuous illumination.
evidence: The abstract provides specific resolution and time measurements for super-resolution imaging.

claim: Most bio-molecules and fluorophores are not able to cross the cell membrane of a living cell.
source: However, most of these bio-molecules and fluorophores are not able to cross the cell membrane of a living cell, making it challenging to image intracellular proteins.
evidence: This is stated as a general limitation in the introduction.

claim: Cell-permeant fluorophores attached to membrane-permeant entities have obvious trade-offs of limited choice in emission wavelengths and available class of ligands.
source: There are a few exceptions to this barrier, namely, by using few selected cell-permeant fluorophores that have been attached to membrane-permeant entities (Lukinavičius et al., 2014; Grimm et al., 2015; Wombacher et al., 2010). These have obvious trade-offs of limited choice in emission wavelengths and available class of ligands that they can be covalently attached to and maintain their selectivity for the particular intracellular protein.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of existing methods, supported by citations.

claim: There has been mixed success in delivering fluorescent probes by appending a membrane-permeant small peptide such as the TAT-TAR HIV peptide.
source: There has also been mixed success in delivering fluorescent probes by appending a membrane-permeant small peptide such as the TAT-TAR HIV peptide (Silhol et al., 2002; Richard et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of existing methods, supported by citations.

claim: Fluorescent proteins (FPs) have limited photostability.
source: In addition, the detection of FPs is less than optimal because of their limited photostability.
evidence: This is stated as a known limitation of fluorescent proteins.

claim: Microinjection, electroporation and osmotic pinosomelysis have significant drawbacks such as low throughput and the requirement of additional apparatus.
source: Other methods that attempt to overcome this limitation include microinjection, electroporation and osmotic pinosomelysis (Okada and Rechsteiner, 1982; Crawford et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 1990; Kim et al., 2008). However, these techniques have significant drawbacks such as low throughput and the requirement of additional apparatus.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of existing methods, supported by citations.

claim: BLAST and cell squeezing require cells to be cultured in specific platforms like fabricated surface or microfluidic channels.
source: Finally, two recently developed methods, such as 'biophotonic laser-assisted surgery tool (BLAST)' and 'cell squeezing' are promising techniques, although they require the cells to be cultured in specific platforms like fabricated surface or microfluidic channels (Wu et al., 2015; Kollmannsperger et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of these methods, supported by citations.

claim: SLO has been used in the past for delivering fluorescently labeled proteins—but not targeted to specific proteins.
source: In the past, SLO has been used for delivering fluorescently labeled proteins—but not targeted to specific proteins (Walev et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated as prior work, supported by a citation.

claim: SLO has been used with transfected cells to deliver a small lanthanide probe.
source: SLO has also been used with transfected cells to deliver a small lanthanide probe (Rajapakse et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as prior work, supported by a citation.

claim: SLO has been used for labeling RNA with 'molecular beacons' or a streptavidin-RNA probe, and also to introduce (non-fluorescent) ligands through the membrane.
source: It has also been used for labeling RNA with 'molecular beacons' or a streptavidin-RNA probe, and also to introduce (non-fluorescent) ligands through the membrane (Nitin and Bao, 2008; Kano et al., 2000; Santangelo et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as prior work, supported by citations.

claim: SLO creates pores of ~30 nm in size.
source: We applied SLO to permeabilized the cells, creating pores of ~30 nm in size (Stewart et al., 2015) in order to deliver fluorescent probes for labeling intracellular proteins in a site-specific manner (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the pore size.

claim: Cells were permeabilized with SLO at 37°C for 7–10 min depending on the cell confluency.
source: First, we permeabilized the cells with SLO at 37°C for 7–10 min depending on the cell confluency, followed by incubation with the fluorescent probes (i.e., fluorophores by themselves, or covalently attached to a ligand or a protein) for 5 min on ice.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol used.

claim: Fluorescent probes were incubated for 5 min on ice after SLO permeabilization.
source: First, we permeabilized the cells with SLO at 37°C for 7–10 min depending on the cell confluency, followed by incubation with the fluorescent probes (i.e., fluorophores by themselves, or covalently attached to a ligand or a protein) for 5 min on ice.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol used.

claim: Cells were allowed to recover in the incubator at 37°C for 15–20 min after SLO treatment.
source: The cells were then allowed to recover in the incubator at 37°C for 15–20 min.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol used.

claim: For super-resolution microscopy (dSTORM), 4 mM glutathione and 0.5 U/mL of Oxyrase were added to create blinking fluorophores.
source: For super-resolution microscopy, namely direct-STORM (dSTORM), 4 mM glutathione and 0.5 U/mL of Oxyrase were added to create blinking fluorophores (Heilemann et al., 2008).
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol used, with a citation for the dSTORM method.

claim: 94% (15 out of 16 cells) of SLO treated cells showed nuclear staining by DAPI.
source: Fluorescence images of SLO treated cells (Figure 1b) revealed 94% (15 out of 16 cells) of the cells in the field of view contains nuclear staining by DAPI, 88% of the cells contains clear and punctate structure of labeled peroxisomes, and 88% of the cells showed filamentous structure of the actin – a stark contrast to SLO untreated negative control cells (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experiment shown in Figure 1b.

claim: 88% of SLO treated cells showed clear and punctate structure of labeled peroxisomes.
source: Fluorescence images of SLO treated cells (Figure 1b) revealed 94% (15 out of 16 cells) of the cells in the field of view contains nuclear staining by DAPI, 88% of the cells contains clear and punctate structure of labeled peroxisomes, and 88% of the cells showed filamentous structure of the actin – a stark contrast to SLO untreated negative control cells (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experiment shown in Figure 1b.

claim: 88% of SLO treated cells showed filamentous structure of the actin.
source: Fluorescence images of SLO treated cells (Figure 1b) revealed 94% (15 out of 16 cells) of the cells in the field of view contains nuclear staining by DAPI, 88% of the cells contains clear and punctate structure of labeled peroxisomes, and 88% of the cells showed filamentous structure of the actin – a stark contrast to SLO untreated negative control cells (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experiment shown in Figure 1b.

claim: The membrane of recovered cells efficiently excluded Texas Red dextran (~20 kDa).
source: To confirm the membrane integrity after recovery, SLO-treated cells were incubated for 5 min with Texas Red dextran, (~20 kDa), a normally membrane-impermeant fluorescent molecule. The membrane of recovered cells efficiently excluded Texas Red dextran (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is an observation from the experiment shown in Figure 1b demonstrating membrane recovery.

claim: Close to 95% of cells had intact membrane after recovery when recovered in proper buffers.
source: We showed that close to 95% of cells had intact membrane after recovery when recovered in proper buffers (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a); that the cells were able to divide (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b); and the cellular organelle displayed comparable morphology before and after SLO treatment (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the viability assay shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Cells were able to divide after SLO treatment.
source: We showed that close to 95% of cells had intact membrane after recovery when recovered in proper buffers (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a); that the cells were able to divide (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b); and the cellular organelle displayed comparable morphology before and after SLO treatment (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is an observation from the cell division assay shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Cellular organelles displayed comparable morphology before and after SLO treatment.
source: We showed that close to 95% of cells had intact membrane after recovery when recovered in proper buffers (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a); that the cells were able to divide (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b); and the cellular organelle displayed comparable morphology before and after SLO treatment (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is an observation from the morphology comparison shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c.

claim: The level of response to TNF-α in SLO-treated cells is comparable to untreated cells.
source: This p65-translocation result shows that the level of response to TNF-α in SLO-treated cells is comparable to untreated cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the p65 translocation assay data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: GBP-ATTO647N (~14 kDa) was able to passively diffuse across the nuclear membrane to label the nuclear protein PCNA-GFP.
source: We found that GBP-ATTO647N (~14 kDa) was able to passively diffuse across the nuclear membrane, or diffuse through the nucleus pore complex, in order to label the nuclear proteins PCNA-GFP.
evidence: This is an observation from the experiment shown in Figure 2.

claim: 40 kDa FITC-dextran was able to access nucleus.
source: In a separate test we found that 40 kDa FITC-dextran was able to access nucleus as well.
evidence: This is an observation from the experiment shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Probes larger than GBP, such as streptavidin (labeled SA, 53 kDa) or 70 kDa FITC-dextran, were not able to passively diffuse across the nuclear membrane.
source: In contrast, probes larger than GBP, such as streptavidin (labeled SA, 53 kDa) or 70 kDa FITC-dextran (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a), were not able to passively diffuse across the nuclear membrane.
evidence: This is an observation from the experiment shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1a.

claim: The cut-off for passive diffusion into nuclear pores is between 40–56 kDa.
source: This cut-off for passive diffusion between 40–56 kDa is consistent with the known size-limit for diffusion into nuclear pores (Grünwald et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and supported by a citation.

claim: Using small probes (<2 kDa) resulted in background-free labeling because the unbound probe diffused out during the recovery phase.
source: Surprisingly, we discovered that using small probes, <2 kDa, resulted in background-free labeling—that is, the unbound probe diffused out during the recovery phase.
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments.

claim: Large molecules (>20 kDa dextran or other similar-sized proteins) remained in the cytoplasm, creating evenly distributed fluorescence across the cytosol.
source: On the other hand, 'large' molecules, >20 kDa dextran or other similar-sized proteins, remained in the cytoplasm, creating evenly distributed fluorescence across the cytosol (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is an observation from the experiment shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claim: The pore formed by SLO allows fluorescently labeled proteins free access to entering the cell, while allowing free access for exit only for relatively small (<2 kDa) proteins.
source: Apparently, the pore formed by SLO allows the fluorescently labeled proteins free access to entering the cell, while allowing free access for exit only for relatively small (<2 kDa) proteins.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observations about probe retention.

claim: Some of the larger probes do get washed out, but not fast enough before the membrane starts to heal, and only smaller probes are given enough time to diffuse out completely.
source: To explain this observation, we hypothesize that some of the larger probes do get washed out, but not fast enough before the membrane starts to heal, and only smaller probes are given enough time to be diffuse out completely.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed to explain the observed differential retention of probes.

claim: The required concentration of fluorescent chloroalkane with SLO-treated cells was a factor of ten lower than that recommended by the manufacturer.
source: In addition, the required concentration of fluorescent chloroalkane with SLO-treated cells was a factor of ten lower than that recommended by the manufacturer.
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments comparing to manufacturer recommendations.

claim: The manufacturer's means of getting the ligand into the cell depends on setting up a concentration gradient across the cell membrane, whereas none is necessary with SLO.
source: This might be because the manufacturer's means of getting the ligand into the cell depends on setting up a concentration gradient across the cell membrane, whereas none is necessary with SLO.
evidence: This is an inference to explain the lower concentration requirement.

claim: A thick actin bundle split over the course of ~3 min into two separate strands, ~850 nm apart using live super-resolution approach.
source: Finally, we observed a thick actin bundle split over the course of ~3 min into two separate strands, ~850 nm apart using this live super-resolution approach (Figure 3c, Video 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the live dSTORM imaging shown in Figure 3c and Video 1.

claim: Phalloidin is an actin stabilizer and will interfere with the normal dynamic of actin.
source: Note that phalloidin is an actin stabilizer and certainly will interfere with the normal dynamic of actin.
evidence: This is stated as a known property of phalloidin.

claim: The signal can be improved ~6-fold by detecting the signal of GBP-ATTO647N than the GFP itself.
source: For instance, we show that the signal can be improved ~6-fold by detecting the signal of GBP-ATTO647N than the GFP itself (Figure 3—figure supplement 3a–b).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experiment shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3a–b.

claim: The average run length and velocity of kinesin was determined to be 621 ± 99 nm (Decay constant ± SE) and 1058 ± 22 nm/s (Center ± SEM) at 30°C.
source: The average run length and velocity was determined to be 621 ± 99 nm (Decay constant ± SE) and 1058 ± 22 nm/s (Center ± SEM) at 30°C (Figure 3f).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the kinesin tracking experiment shown in Figure 3f.

claim: The measured run length and velocity of kinesin agrees with the in vitro data on single kinesin at 30°C.
source: Both the run length and velocity agrees with the in vitro data on single kinesin at 30°C (Kawaguchi and Ishiwata, 2000).
evidence: This is a comparison to published in vitro data, supported by a citation.

claim: A decrease in kinesin velocity was observed at room temperature compared to 30°C.
source: In addition, we have performed the experiment at room temperature, and indeed we observed a decrease in kinesin velocity (Figure 3—figure supplement 3d–e).
evidence: This is an observation from the experiment shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3d–e.

claim: SLO has been applied to label cells without transfection by labeling intracellular proteins with antibodies, nanobodies, and bio-specific ligands.
source: Importantly, we have applied SLO to label cells without transfection. This is achieved by labeling intracellular proteins with antibodies, nanobodies, and bio-specific ligands.
evidence: This is stated as an achievement of the study.

claim: The SLO delivery technique can easily be combined with other signal enhancement techniques, such as 'spaghetti monster', for delivering otherwise membrane impermeant probes into living cells.
source: Our SLO delivery technique can easily be combined with other signal enhancement techniques, such as 'spaghetti monster' (Viswanathan et al., 2015), for delivering otherwise membrane impermeant probes into living cells for labeling a single protein with numerous probes at once.
evidence: This is stated as a potential application, supported by a citation.

claim: The technique can potentially be extended to other types of microscopy that relies on probe delivery, such as cryo-electron microscopy.
source: Lastly, this technique is not limited to delivering of fluorescent probes; the technique can potentially be extended to other types of microscopy that relies on probe delivery, such as cryo-electron microscopy.
evidence: This is stated as a potential future application.

claim: Different batches of SLO may have different activity.
source: Different batches of SLO may have different activity, and therefore the optimal SLO concentration should first be determined.
evidence: This is stated as a practical consideration for the method.

claim: The optimized working SLO concentration was determined by testing a range of SLO concentrations for each cell line to achieve >75% permeability to 10 kDa FITC-dextran, while keeping dead cells at a minimum (<10%).
source: The optimized working SLO concentration was determined by testing a range of SLO concentrations for each cell line to achieve >75% permeability to 10 kDa FITC-dextran, while keeping dead cells at a minimum (<10%).
evidence: This describes the optimization criteria used in the method.

claim: Different cell lines required different dosage of SLO.
source: Different cell lines required different dosage of SLO; a table of SLO dilution to use for a few selected cell lines and confluency is included in Table 1.
evidence: This is stated as an observation, with specific data provided in Table 1.

claim: Permeabilized cells were observed under phase contrast microscopy at 20x magnification after 5 min, where granules inside the cells become more distinctive.
source: Permeabilized cells were observed under phase contrast microscopy at 20x magnification after 5 min. Granules inside the cells become more distinctive in permeabilized cells.
evidence: This describes an observation used to confirm permeabilization.

claim: The number of cells increased by nearly 60% after 16 hr despite SLO treatment, suggesting cells were able to undergo cell division.
source: The number of cells increased by nearly 60% despite SLO treatment, suggesting cells were able to undergo cell division [N=2 regions of interest].
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the cell division assay shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b.

claim: The morphology of mitochondria did not appear to differ after the permeabilization and labeling procedure.
source: The morphology of mitochondria did not appear to differ after the permeabilization and labeling procedure.
evidence: This is an observation from the morphology comparison shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Only recovery media and 10% FBS DMEM successfully resealed the cells to prevent PI staining.
source: Only recovery media and 10% FBS DMEM successfully resealed the cells to prevent PI staining.
evidence: This is an observation from the propidium iodide assay shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a.

claim: There is an initial loss of some metabolites from inside the permeabilized cells.

claim: A larger proportion of molecular motors were immobile along the microtubules in severely permeabilized cells.
source: This is evident from the fact that a larger proportion of molecular motors were immobile along the microtubules in severely permeabilized cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 3b).
evidence: This is an observation from the experiment shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3b.

claim: The effect from the lost metabolites can be rescued by using recovery media which is supplemented with essential metabolites (ATP, GTP and glucose), but not with 10% FBS DMEM.
source: The effect from the lost metabolites can be rescued by using our recovery media which is supplemented with essential metabolites (ATP, GTP and glucose), but not with 10% FBS DMEM.
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments comparing different recovery media.

claim: With the addition of 4 mM glutathione in the recovery media after SLO permeabilization, there are a greater number of activation events detected per frame.
source: With the addition of 4 mM glutathione in the recovery media after SLO permeabilization, there are a greater number of activation events detected per frame, as well as a fewer number of detected events during illumination, suggesting that the added glutathione assists in turning off the fluorophore more efficiently.
evidence: This is an observation from the experiment shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The added glutathione assists in turning off the fluorophore more efficiently.
source: With the addition of 4 mM glutathione in the recovery media after SLO permeabilization, there are a greater number of activation events detected per frame, as well as a fewer number of detected events during illumination, suggesting that the added glutathione assists in turning off the fluorophore more efficiently.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of activation events shown in Figure 3a.

source: The movie was recorded for a total of 20,000 frames at 100 ms exposure time, for a total acquisition time of over 30 min.

claim: No reactivation of Alexa647 was observed without addition of Oxyrase on fixed cell.

source: Activation of Alexa647 on actin in fixed cells and in live cells in the presence of Oxyrase.
